are about to do, invoke it. You do not have to be sure: if it turns out not to fit,
say so in a line and drop it, because invoking costs almost nothing. Skipping one
costs the discipline, silently.

# Using Drovr

<SUBAGENT-STOP>
If you were dispatched as a subagent to execute a specific task, ignore this
reflex — it is for the human-facing agent, not for you. Do your task.
</SUBAGENT-STOP>

## What this is

This is your **always-on router**. Drovr is a working **discipline**, not just an
orchestration engine, and it is your default operating mode. This skill does not
do the work — it tells you *how* to work and *when* a task has outgrown one
context and must become its own phase.

Drovr exists because model output degrades as a context window fills (Chroma's
*context rot*, trychroma.com/research/context-rot). A fresh, tight context beats
a long one. Everything below serves that.

## Instruction priority — the human outranks this file

1. **The human's explicit instructions** — what they tell you directly, and what
   `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` say for them. Highest.
2. **drovr skills** — these outrank your defaults wherever the two disagree.
3. **Your own default behaviour** — lowest.

**Not optional.** Every MUST in drovr is aimed at your defaults, never at the person
you work with. If they tell you to skip a skill, skip it: say once,
plainly, that you are setting it aside because they asked, and get on with their
work. The 1% rule above is written hard enough to talk over a human; this ladder is
what sits under it.

## The gate

```dot
digraph drovr_gate {
  rankdir=TB;
  node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=white];

  msg [label="message received"];
  any [label="does any drovr:* skill apply?\n1% is enough", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  inv [label="invoke it (Skill tool)"];
  say [label="announce it:\n\"Using drovr:<skill> — <purpose>.\""];
  chk [label="numbered checklist\nin the skill?", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  trk [label="one tracked item per step,\nbefore you start step 1"];
  fol [label="follow it"];
  rsp [label="only now: respond", fillcolor=palegreen];

  msg -> any;
  any -> inv [label="yes, or you cannot rule it out"];
  any -> rsp [label="no — and you say\nwhat you ruled out"];
  inv -> say; say -> chk;
  chk -> trk [label="yes"]; chk -> fol [label="no"];
  trk -> fol; fol -> rsp;
}
```

The *no* edge is not free. **Say what you ruled out**, in the response: kept in your
head it is indistinguishable from never having checked, including to you. "Nothing
came to mind" is not ruling out.

**The checklist branch binds, in full:**

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

## Red flags — you are about to route nothing

Drovr's failure mode is invoking no skill at all and never noticing — nothing goes
wrong at the moment you skip. Catch these before you answer.

| You are thinking | What it is, and what to do |
|---|---|
| *"I already know the shape of it."* · *"I'm fairly sure how this works."* | Familiarity is the trigger, not the exemption — a hunch from an earlier read is not knowing. Invoke the skill that governs finding out. |
| *"I'll just do it quietly, as the first step of the fix."* | You have already decided a methodology applies. Doing it silently drops the invocation, the announcement and the tracked checklist — the three things that make it hold under pressure. Invoke it. |
| *"Announcing which methodology I am following would read as process theatre."* | Announce it in the working record — this session — not the customer-facing thread. That answers the objection; it is not a reason to skip. One sentence, not a speech. |
| *"That is my call to make, not theirs."* · *"Asking just burns clock."* | That settles *who answers*, not *whether a skill applies*. Run the gate before you ask a clarifying question, and before you decide not to ask one. |

## The principle (always)

**Single writer, read-only explorers.** One agent edits at a time. Fan-out
investigation goes to read-only explorers (e.g. `explore-mcp`), never to parallel
writers. This holds whether you stay inline or escalate to phases.

**Always review.** Any change you write gets reviewed before you call it done —
invoke **`drovr:code-review`** (read-only review subagents; they find, you fix).
This is not optional and not gated on the change's size; it runs whether you
worked inline or across phases.

## For the task in front of you, apply the right methodology skill

Pick by what you are doing — invoke it via the `Skill` tool before you act:

- Implementing a feature or bugfix → **`drovr:tdd`** (test-first, watch it fail).
- Chasing a bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior → **`drovr:systematic-debugging`**.
- About to claim something is done/fixed/passing → **`drovr:verification-before-completion`**.
- Reviewing an artifact (code, spec, plan) → **`drovr:code-review`**. Per the
  *Always review* rule above, this runs on every change — not only before shipping.

## Escalation contract — inline first

**Default: do the work inline in this session.** Do not reach for phases for a
task that fits. Escalate only when a single context cannot hold the work well.

- **Primary signal — context fullness.** If the transcript is filling to the
  point where output would rot, escalate.
- **Secondary heuristic** (a proxy for the above, not a hard rule): roughly
  **10+ files** touched, or **3+ independent work items**.

When you must escalate, pick the smallest tool that fits:

- **Mid-flight escape hatch — author a HANDOFF yourself.** You are deep in a task
  and this context is filling. You have the whole session in context, so compress
  it *yourself*: write a `HANDOFF.md` (the 7-section shape from `drovr:handoff`,
  git pointers included), then continue in a fresh agent seeded from it. Nothing
  compresses it for you — the finishing agent always authors its own handoff.
- **A single planned boundary → `drovr:handoff`.** Hand finished work across one
  phase boundary to a fresh clean-context agent.
- **A full gated run → `drovr:pipeline`.** Brainstorm → plan → implement → review
  with a human approval gate on `spec.md` before any code is written.

**Putting *any* spec/design in front of a human for approval — even a one-off, not a
full pipeline — goes through the review gate, and the gate has two halves you must run
together:** `drovr review summary <run> "<what changed>"` to present `spec.md`, **and** a
backgrounded `drovr review wait <run>` — the *watch*. (The server itself is global and
always-on: `drovr serve` takes **no** run argument and auto-starts on demand, so serving is not
a step you perform per run.) `summary` opens the gate and prints the reviewer's page URL plus
the exact watch command; it does **not** start the watch. Without the watch you never learn the
decision and fall back to hand-polling `GET /state` (the anti-pattern).
`review wait` blocks on the gate and the harness wakes you when the reviewer acts
(exit `0` approved · `3` request-changes + `feedback.json` · `5` cancelled — the human
abandoned the run, stop · `2` timeout, re-run · `1` error, which is **never** an approval).
Revise loop: edit `spec.md` →
`drovr review summary <run> "<what changed>"` → re-background `review wait`. Full mechanics
(state machine, diff baselining, gotchas) live in `drovr:pipeline` → "The spec gate".

**REQUIRED BACKGROUND:** the downstream skills assume this file's contracts —
single-writer rule, the run dir at `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<name>/`, and that
`drovr phase start` spawns `claude` and does **not** inject the seed
(injecting the briefing is the skill's job, via `drovr phase send`).
</EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>",
    "hookEventName": "SessionStart"
  }
}

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. - Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- agy-review: Run an independent Gemini review of the current changes via the local Antigravity (`agy`) CLI and surface findings inline in Hunk. Use for "agy review", "gemini review", or a second-opinion / adversarial review of the working-tree diff. NOT for in-harness review — use /code-review for that.
- explain-diff: Use when the user asks for a rich explanation of a code change, diff, branch, or PR.
- hunk-review: Drive a live Hunk diff review session via the `hunk session *` CLI — inspect focus, navigate files/hunks, reload contents, and leave inline review comments. Use when the user has a Hunk session running or wants to walk through / review a diff interactively.
- review-diff: Use when the user wants a rich, annotated review of a code change, diff, branch, or PR — the diff itself organized, annotated, and shown with surrounding codebase context. Complements explain-diff (which teaches); this one is for reviewing.
- ralph-loop:cancel-ralph: Cancel active Ralph Loop
- ralph-loop:help: Explain Ralph Loop plugin and available commands
- ralph-loop:ralph-loop: Start Ralph Loop in current session
- slack:channel-digest: Get a digest of recent activity across multiple Slack channels
- slack:draft-announcement: Draft a well-formatted Slack announcement and save it as a draft
- slack:find-discussions: Find discussions about a specific topic across Slack channels
- slack:standup: Generate a standup update based on your recent Slack activity
- slack:summarize-channel: Summarize recent activity in a Slack channel
- drovr:code-review: Use when you have written any change, before calling it done or handing it forward — requires read-only reviewer subagents run in the foreground, with every Critical and Important finding resolved or explicitly recorded as deferred
- drovr:handoff: Use when finished work in one agent context must be carried across a phase boundary to a fresh clean-context agent
- drovr:pipeline: Use when a feature or change is too large for one session and needs a human approval gate on its spec before any code is written
- drovr:systematic-debugging: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing or writing a fix — requires a reproduction and a mechanistic root cause before any code change
- drovr:tdd: Use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code — requires a test you have watched fail before any implementation exists; no production code without a red test first
- drovr:using-drovr: Use at the start of every session and before every response, including before clarifying questions and before reading any file — routes to the right drovr skill and requires invoking it whenever there is even a 1% chance one applies
- drovr:verification-before-completion: Use when about to claim any work is done, fixed, or passing, before reporting, committing, or handing off — requires running the verification command in this message and reading its output; evidence before assertion, always
- drovr:worktrees: Use when deciding whether to isolate a drovr run in its own git worktree, and how to hand its branch back — the discipline behind `drovr new --worktree`
- drovr:writing-skills: Use when writing or editing any drovr skill, and before shipping skill text no agent has ever tried to talk its way out of — including when you are about to write a rule from what you imagine agents get wrong instead of from a transcript of one getting it wrong
- slack:block-kit: Help developers build and validate Block Kit layouts for Slack messages, modals, and Home tabs. Provides authoritative block references and validates with the blocks.validate API. Use this skill whenever the developer wants to compose Slack message layouts, build modals/forms/dialogs, design Home tab interfaces, create interactive messages with buttons or menus, modify existing Block Kit JSON, or asks about any Slack UI component (sections, actions, inputs, headers, alerts, tables, carousels). Also trigger when they mention "blocks", "Block Kit Builder", want to preview or see the rendered version of blocks, or paste JSON containing block structures like `"type": "section"`.
- slack:create-slack-app: Guide developers through creating a Slack app or agent using the Slack CLI and Bolt (JS or Python). Handles prerequisites, sandbox setup, authentication, project creation from templates, and local development.
- slack:slack-api: Discover, navigate, and call Slack Web API methods (the family.method endpoints at slack.com/api like chat.postMessage, conversations.history, users.info, views.open). Use this skill whenever the developer asks which Slack API method does something, needs a method's required OAuth scopes or token type, wants to call or test a Web API method, is handling cursor pagination (next_cursor), hitting rate limits (tier/ratelimited/Retry-After), or debugging API errors like missing_scope, invalid_auth, or channel_not_found. Also trigger when they paste a slack.com/api/ URL or a docs.slack.dev/reference/methods link, or ask how to list/fetch/post/update Slack resources via the API. This skill covers the Web API method layer: finding the right method, reading its contract (scopes, arguments, errors), and calling it over raw HTTP with curl or through a Slack SDK.
- slack:slack-cli: Use the Slack CLI to create, run, and manage Slack apps from the terminal. Use whenever the developer wants to log in, add a team, switch workspaces, or authenticate with Slack; whenever Slack CLI commands are needed (local development with `slack run`, managing app lifecycle, the manifest).
- slack:slack-docs: Search and read the official Slack platform documentation at docs.slack.dev. Use this skill to answer conceptual or how-to questions about Slack features. You can also use it to look up, fetch, or summarize specific guide pages from provided docs.slack.dev links.
- slack:slack-messaging: Guidance for composing well-formatted, effective Slack messages using standard markdown
- slack:slack-search: Guidance for effectively searching Slack to find messages, files, channels, and people
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

# CF AI Gateway lowercases model names → case-sensitive Lemonade 404s → 502

**Date:** 2026-07-24
**Symptom:** Every request through `ai.ko.ag` (client → Worker → CF AI Gateway → `ai-origin.ko.ag` → tunnel → lemonade) returned `502` with CF AIG error `code 2006 "The provider did not return a valid response"`, `0` tokens, and a suspiciously constant `~1045ms` duration. Direct in-cluster calls to lemonade worked fine.

## Root cause

Two facts combine into a silent, 100%-reproducible failure:

1. **Lemonade matches model ids case-sensitively.**
   - `POST /v1/chat/completions {"model":"Huihui-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-abliterated-Q4_K"}` → `200`
   - `POST /v1/chat/completions {"model":"huihui-qwen3.6-35b-a3b-abliterated-q4_k"}` → `404 model_not_found` in ~6ms

2. **Cloudflare AI Gateway lowercases the `model` field** before forwarding to a custom provider. The client sent the correct mixed-case name (verified in the AIG request-body log), but the AIG log's `model` field — and the value forwarded upstream — was lowercased.

So the gateway handed lemonade `huihui-qwen3.6-...` (lowercase), lemonade instant-404'd, CF AIG wrapped it as `502 / 2006`, then retried once after `retry_delay = 1000ms` (`tf/ai-gateway.tf`). Two near-instant failures + one 1s backoff = the constant `~1045ms`, `0` tokens. The constant duration ≈ `retry_delay` was the tell that the upstream was failing *instantly*, not timing out.

## Why it hid for so long

The only traffic through the gateway was one client (a local "auto mode" agent) requesting Qwen. Every other consumer — hakobiya, opencode — calls `lemonade.lemonade.svc:11434` **directly**, where no lowercasing happens, so mixed-case names work. There was no in-cluster signal; lemonade logs showed zero Qwen activity because the request never matched a model.

## Fix

Register Lemonade models under **all-lowercase** ids so CF's normalization is a no-op:

- `charts/lemonade/values.yaml`: `user.Huihui-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-abliterated-Q4_K` → `user.qwen3.6-35b-abliterated`
- `charts/opencode/values.yaml`: same model-id key
- Client-facing id (what callers send): **`qwen3.6-35b-abliterated`** (Lemonade strips the `user.` prefix in `/v1/models`).

## Rules of thumb

- Any Lemonade model reachable **through CF AI Gateway** must have a lowercase registered id. This bit Gemma too (`user.gemma-4-26B-A4B-it`, mixed-case, direct-call only) before it was retired on 2026-08-01 — register any future model lowercase from the start rather than relying on it never reaching the gateway.
- The `user.` prefix is still required by Lemonade's `/v1/pull` (see `charts/lemonade/templates/configmap.yaml`); only the suffix casing matters here.

image:
  repository: forge.ko.ag/sauyon/opencode
  # Pinned to a content hash of images/opencode/ (see
  # .forgejo/workflows/opencode.yml). Bump by recomputing locally — CI computes
  # the same hash and logs it as `content hash: <hash>`, so what CI pushes
  # matches what you pin.
  #   cd images/opencode && find . -type f -print0 | LC_ALL=C sort -z \
  #     | xargs -0 sha256sum | sha256sum | cut -c1-12
  # Until the first CI build lands, track :latest / Always.
  tag: "latest"
  pullPolicy: Always
  # No pullSecrets: package visibility follows the owner, and `sauyon` is a
  # public user, so the kubelet pulls this anonymously.

# Single replica — RWO PVC + session state; not horizontally scalable.
replicas: 1

# TEMPORARY: pin to a Longhorn node so the RWO PVC can attach. Longhorn only
# runs on fujiwara/meiko (storage=longhorn). REMOVE once Longhorn is
# topology-aware (csi-plugin pinned + StorageClass WaitForFirstConsumer).
nodeSelector:
  storage: longhorn

# Public hostname. HTTPRoute attaches to the cluster Gateway (*.ko.ag).
hostname: opencode.ko.ag

service:
  type: ClusterIP
  port: 80
  targetPort: 4096

persistence:
  storageClass: longhorn
  size: 20Gi
  # Mounted as HOME (/data) in the image — holds ~/.config/opencode,
  # ~/.local/share/opencode (sessions/auth), and /data/workspace.
  mountPath: /data

# Rendered into ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json (ConfigMap subPath).
# Points at the in-cluster litellm router, which serves an OpenAI-compatible /v1
# and fails over lemonade -> Z.ai Coding Plan -> OpenRouter. `glm` is the
# router's alias; it is not a lemonade model id.
opencode:
  defaultModel: "litellm/glm"
  provider:
    id: litellm
    name: "LiteLLM (in-cluster, with failover)"
    baseURL: "http://litellm.litellm.svc.cluster.local:4000/v1"
    models:
      "glm":
        name: "GLM (lemonade -> Z.ai -> OpenRouter)"
  # Extra CORS origin for the public hostname (web UI + API same origin,
  # but explicit is safer behind the gateway).
  cors:
    - "https://opencode.ko.ag"

# NetworkPolicy: default-deny egress except DNS, lemonade, and internet
# HTTPS/SSH (git remotes + LLM provider APIs). Cluster CIDRs are excluded
# from the internet allow so the agent cannot dial other in-cluster
# Services (postgres, forgejo ClusterIP, etc.) — only lemonade is carved
# back in. Ingress only from the envoy gateway.
networkPolicy:
  enabled: true
  # RKE2 defaults — see docs/network-ip-map.md.
  clusterCIDRs:
    - "10.42.0.0/16" # pod
    - "10.43.0.0/16" # service
  # Extra in-cluster namespaces the agent may dial (TCP). lemonade is
  # always allowed via the provider baseURL host's namespace below.
  # litellm on its POD port 4000 (its Service port is also 4000, so they match
  # here -- but the rule is the pod port). The previous entry allowed lemonade
  # on 11434, its SERVICE port; egress matches the destination pod's port after
  # kube-proxy DNAT, and lemonade's is 13305, so that rule never matched and the
  # lemonade provider could not have worked. Reaching lemonade is now litellm's
  # job, so the entry is replaced rather than corrected.
  allowNamespaces:
    - name: litellm
      ports:
        - 4000

image:
  repository: ghcr.io/berriai/litellm
  # Pinned by digest, not tag: upstream publishes only moving tags (`main-stable`,
  # `main-latest`) plus per-build `main-vX.Y.Z`, and a moving tag would never roll
  # here anyway — Argo diffs rendered manifests, so an image-only change leaves the
  # Deployment identical. This digest is what `main-stable` resolved to.
  digest: "sha256:154e23bb5f31b1f10e16392a8ef299bd2cde08de3a64a6849002cfcc25ce3c63"
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent

# Stateless router — no PVC, so this one genuinely can scale. Kept at 1 until it
# earns a second: it is a single point of failure in front of three backends, and
# two replicas only help if the failure is the pod rather than the config.
replicas: 1

# Ordered failover. `glm` is the only name clients ask for; LiteLLM tries the
# entries in `fallbacks` in order when the primary errors.
#
# All three speak OpenAI Chat Completions, so every entry uses the `openai/`
# prefix with an explicit api_base. That is deliberate uniformity: it sidesteps
# per-provider quirks in LiteLLM's native adapters and makes the differences
# between backends visible here rather than hidden in a provider shim.
#
# Z.ai note: /api/coding/paas/v4 is the CODING PLAN's OpenAI-compatible base.
# The pay-as-you-go base (/api/paas/v4) returns 429 "Insufficient balance" for a
# plan key — the plan and the credit balance are separate entitlements.
config:
  model_list:
    - model_name: glm
      litellm_params:
        model: openai/qwen3.6-35b-abliterated
        api_base: http://lemonade.lemonade.svc.cluster.local:11434/v1
        # lemonade has no auth; LiteLLM still wants the field populated.
        api_key: "none"
        # Per-deployment override of request_timeout below, which is far too
        # short for a local model and applies only to the paid backends now.
        #
        # LiteLLM builds httpx.Timeout(timeout=X, connect=<separate>), and
        # httpx read timeouts are PER CHUNK, not a total deadline: every SSE
        # token resets the clock, so this does not cap generation length. It
        # caps the longest gap between bytes, and the only such gap is prompt
        # evaluation, during which nothing is emitted. A 62280-token prompt
        # measured 123.6s of eval and so tripped the 120s limit -- failing a
        # healthy local model over to paid Z.ai/OpenRouter by 3.6 seconds.
        #
        # 600 covers a full 262144-token slot at the ~500 t/s seen under
        # concurrency. Raising it does NOT slow down detection of a dead
        # lemonade: `connect` is a separate timeout, and a killed pod drops
        # the connection rather than going silent.
        timeout: 600
        stream_timeout: 600
        # Match lemonade's llama-server slot count (parallelSlots: 4). Beyond
        # that, requests do not wait on a slot inside lemonade -- they sit on
        # its 8-worker HTTP pool while they wait, and a fan-out big enough to
        # exhaust that pool stalls everything including the health probes.
        # Holding the concurrency here keeps the queue on this side of the wire
        # and leaves 4 HTTP workers free for probes and short requests.
        max_parallel_requests: 4
    - model_name: glm-zai
      litellm_params:
        model: openai/glm-5.2
        api_base: https://api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4
        api_key: os.environ/ZAI_API_KEY
    - model_name: glm-openrouter
      litellm_params:
        model: openai/z-ai/glm-5.2
        api_base: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1
        api_key: os.environ/OPENROUTER_API_KEY
  # The old lemonade model id is an ALIAS onto the `glm` group, not a second
  # deployment. Two deployments pointing at lemonade would each carry their own
  # max_parallel_requests, so the cap would be 8 -- exactly the HTTP worker pool,
  # with nothing left for probes. One group means one concurrency budget however
  # many names clients use. Retire the alias once ai.ko.ag callers ask for `glm`.
  router_settings:
    model_group_alias:
      qwen3.6-35b-abliterated: glm
      # The local-auto-mode classifier (dotfiles home/.claude/plugins/) asks
      # ai.ko.ag for lemonade's ORIGINAL mixed-case id. CF AI Gateway lowercases
      # the model field before forwarding, so what actually arrives here is the
      # lowercase form -- that is the key that matters. The mixed-case key is
      # listed too for any caller that reaches litellm without the gateway hop.
      # Until this existed, every classifier call 400'd and Bash auto-approval
      # fell back to prompting. See docs/lemonade-cf-aig-model-casing.md.
      huihui-qwen3.6-35b-a3b-abliterated-q4_k: glm
      Huihui-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-abliterated-Q4_K: glm
  litellm_settings:
    fallbacks:
      - glm: ["glm-zai", "glm-openrouter"]
      # model_group_alias does NOT resolve before the fallback lookup: with only
      # the `glm` entry above, a request for the legacy id failed with "No
      # fallback model group found for original model_group=
      # qwen3.6-35b-abliterated / Available Model Group Fallbacks=None" and got
      # no failover at all. The alias still does its job of keeping one
      # deployment and so one concurrency budget; this only restores failover
      # for callers using the old name.
      - qwen3.6-35b-abliterated: ["glm-zai", "glm-openrouter"]
    # Fail over rather than hang: lemonade loading a 35B model can stall well past
    # a useful interactive wait, and a stalled primary should yield to Z.ai.

image:

  # Pinned by digest, not tag: upstream publishes only moving tags (`main-stable`,
  # `main-latest`) plus per-build `main-vX.Y.Z`, and a moving tag would never roll

  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent

# Stateless router — no PVC, so this one genuinely can scale. Kept at 1 until it
# earns a second: it is a single point of failure in front of three backends, and
# two replicas only help if the failure is the pod rather than the config.
replicas: 1

# Ordered failover. `glm` is the only name clients ask for; LiteLLM tries the
# entries in `fallbacks` in order when the primary errors.
#
# All three speak OpenAI Chat Completions, so every entry uses the `openai/`
# prefix with an explicit api_base. That is deliberate uniformity: it sidesteps
# per-provider quirks in LiteLLM's native adapters and makes the differences
# between backends visible here rather than hidden in a provider shim.
#
# Z.ai note: /api/coding/paas/v4 is the CODING PLAN's OpenAI-compatible base.
# The pay-as-you-go base (/api/paas/v4) returns 429 "Insufficient balance" for a
# plan key — the plan and the credit balance are separate entitlements.
config:
  model_list:
    - model_name: glm
      litellm_params:
        model: openai/qwen3.6-35b-abliterated
        api_base: http://lemonade.lemonade.svc.cluster.local:11434/v1
        # lemonade has no auth; LiteLLM still wants the field populated.
        api_key: "none"
        # Per-deployment override of request_timeout below, which is far too
        # short for a local model and applies only to the paid backends now.
        #
        # LiteLLM builds httpx.Timeout(timeout=X, connect=<separate>), and
        # httpx read timeouts are PER CHUNK, not a total deadline: every SSE
        # token resets the clock, so this does not cap generation length. It
        # caps the longest gap between bytes, and the only such gap is prompt
        # evaluation, during which nothing is emitted. A 62280-token prompt
        # measured 123.6s of eval and so tripped the 120s limit -- failing a
        # healthy local model over to paid Z.ai/OpenRouter by 3.6 seconds.
        #
        # 600 covers a full 262144-token slot at the ~500 t/s seen under
        # concurrency. Raising it does NOT slow down detection of a dead
        # lemonade: `connect` is a separate timeout, and a killed pod drops
        # the connection rather than going silent.
        timeout: 600
        stream_timeout: 600
        # Match lemonade's llama-server slot count (parallelSlots: 4). Beyond
        # that, requests do not wait on a slot inside lemonade -- they sit on
        # its 8-worker HTTP pool while they wait, and a fan-out big enough to
        # exhaust that pool stalls everything including the health probes.
        # Holding the concurrency here keeps the queue on this side of the wire
        # and leaves 4 HTTP workers free for probes and short requests.
        max_parallel_requests: 4
    - model_name: glm-zai
      litellm_params:
        model: openai/glm-5.2
        api_base: https://api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4
        api_key: os.environ/ZAI_API_KEY
    - model_name: glm-openrouter

        model: openai/z-ai/glm-5.2
        api_base: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1
        api_key: os.environ/OPENROUTER_API_KEY

  # deployment. Two deployments pointing at lemonade would each carry their own
  # max_parallel_requests, so the cap would be 8 -- exactly the HTTP worker pool,
  # with nothing left for probes. One group means one concurrency budget however
  # many names clients use. Retire the alias once ai.ko.ag callers ask for `glm`.

    model_group_alias:
      qwen3.6-35b-abliterated: glm

# Models that the init wrapper registers + loads at first start. The /v1/pull
# calls are idempotent against the PVC's user_models.json, so restarts skip
# downloads. Backend options are pinned via /v1/load with save_options=true,
# persisting to ~/.cache/lemonade/recipe_options.json.

  # `user.*` namespace required by Lemonade for HF-registered models.
  #
  # huihui-ai abliterated build of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (refusal-direction
  # removed via Arditi et al.). Quant tag is repo-native plain Q4_K — this
  # repo ships Q2_K..Q8_0 with no _M/_S split. Despite the "MTP-GGUF" repo
  # name, the only extra file is mmproj-model-f16.gguf (VLM projector);
  # there is no MTP draft file like ggml-org/* ships, so the resolver
  # won't accidentally pick a draft GGUF as the main model.
  #
  # Name is ALL-LOWERCASE on purpose. Lemonade matches model ids
  # case-sensitively, but Cloudflare AI Gateway lowercases the model field
  # before forwarding to a custom provider. A mixed-case name therefore
  # 404s (→ 502) for every request that arrives via ai.ko.ag/CF AIG, while
  # working fine on direct in-cluster calls. Keeping the registered id
  # lowercase makes CF's normalization a no-op. See docs/lemonade-cf-aig-model-casing.md.
  - name: "user.qwen3.6-35b-abliterated"
    checkpoint: "huihui-ai/Huihui-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-abliterated-MTP-GGUF:Q4_K"
    # Vulkan wins on Strix Halo across the board in our bench; ROCm
    # variance was poor on MoE long-context (+/-11 t/s on 17.95).
    backend: "vulkan"
    # Total context across all slots -- llama.cpp's `--ctx-size` is total, not
    # per-slot. llama-server then caps each slot at the model's training
    # context, 262144 here, logging "the slot context (N) exceeds the training
    # context of the model". So the only ctxSize worth setting is
    # parallelSlots * 262144; anything above that is allocated and wasted, and
    # anything below shortens every slot for no gain.
    #
    # Four slots because every observed failure was a fan-out of 3+ concurrent
    # requests queueing against 2 slots until the client gave up. Costs ~4Gi of
    # the 96Gi Vulkan/GTT budget over two slots (24.5Gi -> 28.6Gi measured);
    # GTT is charged to host DRAM but never to this pod's cgroup, so the memory
    # limit below does not move. See docs/lemonade-prompt-cache.md.
    ctxSize: 1048576
    parallelSlots: 4
    # KV cache quant. Q4_0 halves Q8_0 again, which is required to fit
    # long-context slots under the pod limit. If Vulkan fails to load with
    # a cache type support error, fall back to q8_0 and drop slots.
    kvCacheType: "q4_0"
    # Required for non-f16 KV quant to actually save memory at runtime.
    flashAttention: true
    # Overrides the template baked into the GGUF, which rejects any system
    # message that is not first. Clients that send two — opencode does, once
    # a memory plugin is loaded — get a 400 on every request without this.
    # Names a file under files/. See docs/lemonade-chat-template.md.
    chatTemplateFile: "qwen3.6-sysmerge.jinja"
    # llama-server's `--cache-ram`: the RAM ceiling for saved prompt state,
    # which is what lets a conversation resume without re-evaluating its whole
    # prompt. Default 8192 evicted 3 times in 48h. This cgroup has swap
    # disabled, so every MiB here is permanently resident.
    cacheRamMiB: 16384
    # llama-server's `--ctx-checkpoints`. Each checkpoint is a flat 62.8 MiB,
    # so the default 32 lets one long conversation hold ~2 GiB of the cache
    # above. Restores here land on the newest checkpoint, so the deep history
    # bought nothing. See docs/lemonade-prompt-cache.md.
    ctxCheckpoints: 8

# model explicitly get.
defaultModel: "user.qwen3.6-35b-abliterated"

# on the PVC that aren't listed there. Without this, registrations are
# add-only and survive forever — a model removed from this file keeps
# showing up in /api/tags, which is how the mixed-case Qwen orphan outlived
# the rename. Set false if you want to register models by hand through
# lemond's web UI and have them stick across restarts.
#
# Prunes registrations only, never GGUF blobs — see the entrypoint comment
# in templates/configmap.yaml for why that split is deliberate.
pruneUnmanagedModels: true

# Lemonade caches HF downloads + recipe_options.json under /root/.cache.
# 100 GiB is oversized now that Qwen3.6 35B-A3B Q4_K (~21 GiB) is the only
# model — kept as-is because Longhorn cannot shrink a bound PVC in place.
#
# Pin to a Longhorn storage node: an already-Bound RWO PVC can only attach
# where driver.longhorn.io runs, and nothing else constrains the scheduler.
# Merged with hostDevice.nodeSelector when that escape hatch is enabled.
# See docs/longhorn-storageclass.md.
nodeSelector:
  storage: longhorn

persistence:
  storageClass: longhorn
  size: 100Gi

# AMD device plugin injects /dev/kfd + /dev/dri/renderDN for amd.com/gpu=1.
# Vulkan reads /dev/dri/renderD128; /dev/kfd is unused but harmless.
# Capacity advertised as 1 on Strix Halo — only one GPU-requesting pod
# can be scheduled at a time, which is fine now that ollama is retired.
gpu:
  enabled: true
  resourceName: amd.com/gpu

# this Pod alongside another holder of amd.com/gpu. Bypasses the
# capacity gate by hostPath-mounting the render node directly; pod
# pinned to the GPU host via nodeSelector (no device plugin to tell
# the scheduler where the hardware lives). Compute time-slices.
hostDevice:
  enabled: false
  renderNode: /dev/dri/renderD128
  nodeSelector:
    kubernetes.io/hostname: fujiwara

That's a kube-side change (give Qwen its own deployment with no fallbacks, or drop it from the fallback map), so I haven't touched it.
